concepts.name: Linear momentum, $\kp = m\kv$
concepts.statement: Linear momentum is the product of a system’s mass and its velocity, and it is the quantity that says how hard a moving object is to stop. A large, fast-moving object has greater momentum than a smaller, slower one.

forms.condition: only the magnitude of the momentum is considered

concepts.name: Calculate a momentum from a mass and a velocity
concepts.statement: Momentum is a vector with the same direction as the velocity, and its SI unit is the kilogram meter per second. Multiplying a mass by a velocity, keeping the direction and the unit, gives the momentum from which a collision problem starts.

concepts.name: Newton’s second law in terms of momentum, $\kFnet = \kdp / \kdt$
concepts.statement: Newton stated his second law as the net external force equals the change in momentum of a system divided by the time over which it changes. This is the more general statement, because it holds for a system whose mass changes, such as a rocket, as well as for one whose mass is constant.

concepts.name: The familiar $\kFnet = m\ka$ as the constant-mass case
concepts.statement: When the mass of the system does not change, the change in momentum is the mass times the change in velocity, and dividing by the time gives the acceleration. The familiar form of the second law, $F_{\text{net}} = ma$, is therefore the special case of the momentum form for a constant mass.

forms.condition: the mass of the system is constant

concepts.name: Change in momentum $\kdp$
concepts.statement: The change in momentum is the difference between the final and the initial momentum, and for a constant mass it is the mass times the change in velocity. It is the quantity that a force acting for a time produces.

forms.condition: the mass of the system is constant
the mass of the system is constant

concepts.name: Impulse, $\kdp = \kFnet\kdt$
concepts.statement: Rearranging Newton’s second law shows that the change in momentum equals the average net external force multiplied by the time this force acts, and that product is called the impulse. Impulse is the same as the change in momentum, so the effect of a force depends on how long it acts as well as on how great it is.

forms.condition: the ball strikes the wall along the perpendicular and rebounds with the same speed
the ball strikes the wall at 30° from the perpendicular and rebounds at the same angle with the same speed

concepts.name: A longer collision time means a smaller force
concepts.statement: The change in momentum a stop requires is fixed by the mass and the speed, so if the stop is spread over a longer time the force is smaller. This is why a car has a padded dashboard, an airbag and parts that crumple, and why you roll on landing rather than land stiff-legged.

concepts.name: Average effective force $\kFeff$
concepts.statement: A real force is not constant over the brief time of a collision, but you can always find an average effective force that produces the same result. On a graph of force against time, the area under the actual curve is the impulse, and the rectangle of the effective force over the same interval has the same area.

concepts.name: Find an average force from a change in momentum and a contact time
concepts.statement: The average force of a collision is found from the mass and the velocities before and after it: form the change in momentum, keeping its direction, and divide by the time of contact.

concepts.name: The two changes in momentum cancel, $\Delta \kpone + \Delta \kptwo = 0$
concepts.statement: The two cars push on each other for the same length of time, and Newton’s third law makes the two forces equal and opposite. The impulses are therefore equal and opposite, so the momentum one car loses is the momentum the other gains, and this is the whole argument for conservation of momentum.

concepts.name: Conservation of momentum, $\kptot = \kptotprime$
concepts.statement: The total momentum of an isolated system is constant, whatever happens inside it and however many objects it holds. Momentum is one of the few quantities nature conserves, and every collision in the rest of the chapter is solved by writing the total momentum before the collision equal to the total momentum after it.

forms.condition: the net external force on the two-object system is zero

concepts.name: Isolated system, $\kFnet = 0$
concepts.statement: An isolated system is one for which the net external force is zero, and that is exactly the condition momentum needs in order to be conserved. Before you can use conservation of momentum you have to choose a system large enough that the forces that matter are internal to it.

concepts.name: Recoil
concepts.statement: The backward momentum felt by a body that exerts a force on another is called a recoil. When a football player runs into the goalpost the Earth recoils too, and because the Earth is so much more massive its recoil is immeasurably small, though it is real nevertheless.

concepts.name: Momentum can be conserved along one direction and not another
concepts.statement: The three directions in space are independent, so momentum can be conserved along one of them while it is not conserved along another. For a projectile with negligible air resistance the horizontal forces are zero and the horizontal momentum is unchanged, while the vertical force of gravity is not zero and the vertical momentum is not conserved.

concepts.name: Momentum of subatomic particles
concepts.statement: Conservation of momentum is not a rule about billiard balls alone. Momentum is a property of every subatomic particle, massless ones such as photons included, and the analysis of what scatters from what is how the nucleus and the quarks inside a proton were found.

concepts.name: Quark
concepts.statement: A quark is a fundamental constituent of matter and an elementary particle.

concepts.name: Elastic collision
concepts.statement: An elastic collision is one that conserves internal kinetic energy as well as momentum. That second conservation law is the extra equation you need when both final velocities are unknown, so knowing whether a collision is elastic decides how you can solve it.

forms.condition: the collision is elastic, so internal kinetic energy is conserved

concepts.name: Internal kinetic energy $\kKEint$
concepts.statement: The internal kinetic energy of a system is the sum of the kinetic energies of the objects in it. It is the quantity that is conserved in an elastic collision and changed in an inelastic one, so it is the bookkeeping that tells the two kinds of collision apart.

concepts.name: Find both final velocities of a one-dimensional elastic collision
concepts.statement: Two unknown final velocities need two independent equations, and an elastic collision supplies them: conservation of momentum and conservation of internal kinetic energy. Solving the pair gives a quadratic with two roots, and the root that repeats the initial condition describes the situation before the collision and is discarded.

forms.condition: the second object is initially at rest

concepts.name: Real collisions are at best nearly elastic
concepts.statement: Truly elastic collisions can only be achieved with subatomic particles. Macroscopic collisions always convert some kinetic energy into heat transfer due to friction and into sound, so two steel blocks on ice or two carts with spring bumpers on an air track are treated as elastic because they are nearly so, not because they are exactly so.

concepts.name: Inelastic collision
concepts.statement: An inelastic collision is one in which the internal kinetic energy changes. The forces between the colliding objects do work that can turn internal kinetic energy into heat transfer, or turn stored energy into internal kinetic energy, so only momentum can be counted on here.

concepts.name: Perfectly inelastic collision, $m_1\kvone = (m_1 + m_2)\kvprime$
concepts.statement: A collision in which the objects stick together is called perfectly inelastic, because it reduces internal kinetic energy more than any other kind of collision can while still conserving momentum. Since the two objects share one final velocity afterwards, conservation of momentum alone is enough to find it.

forms.condition: the objects stick together and the second is initially at rest

concepts.name: Recoil velocity, $\kvprime = m_1\kvone / (m_1 + m_2)$
concepts.statement: When a moving object is caught by one that is at rest, the two move off together at the incoming velocity reduced by the ratio of the incoming mass to the total mass. A goalie who catches a puck therefore recoils only a few centimetres a second, which is why the recoil of a heavy body is so easy to miss.

forms.condition: the objects stick together and the second is initially at rest

concepts.name: Find the internal kinetic energy lost in a collision
concepts.statement: Once the final velocities are known you can add up the kinetic energies before the collision and after it and subtract. The difference is what was lost to thermal energy and sound, and in a perfectly inelastic collision it is nearly all of what there was to begin with.

concepts.name: A collision can release stored energy
concepts.statement: An inelastic collision does not only remove internal kinetic energy; it can add it. When a compressed spring is released during the collision, or when exploding bolts push a satellite away from its launcher, stored energy is converted into internal kinetic energy and the system ends with more than it started with.

concepts.name: Two-dimensional collision
concepts.statement: When objects scatter to the side rather than along one line, you choose a convenient coordinate system and resolve the motion into components along perpendicular axes. Resolving the motion this way yields a pair of one-dimensional problems to be solved together, which is the same approach that carried kinematics and dynamics into the plane.

concepts.name: Point mass
concepts.statement: Two objects that collide off centre can begin to spin, and rotation is not treated until later. A point mass is a structureless particle that cannot rotate or spin, and restricting the analysis to point masses is what keeps the collision describable by the velocities alone.

concepts.name: Momentum along the x-axis, $m_1\kvone = m_1\kvoneprime\cos\theta_1 + m_2\kvtwoprime\cos\theta_2$
concepts.statement: With the x-axis chosen parallel to the velocity of the incoming object and the second object at rest, the whole of the initial momentum lies along x. Conservation of momentum along that axis then relates the one initial speed to the two final speeds and the two scattering angles.

forms.condition: the second object is initially at rest and the x-axis is parallel to the velocity of the incoming object

concepts.name: Momentum along the y-axis, $0 = m_1\kvoneprime\sin\theta_1 + m_2\kvtwoprime\sin\theta_2$
concepts.statement: Neither object has any momentum along the y-axis before the collision, so the two y-components afterwards must add to zero. This is the second of the two independent equations, and it is the one that ties the two scattering angles to each other.

forms.condition: the second object is initially at rest and the x-axis is parallel to the velocity of the incoming object

concepts.name: Find an unseen object’s velocity from the scattering of another
concepts.statement: Two equations can be solved for two unknowns. Taking the ratio of the two conservation equations removes the unknown speed and leaves the unknown angle, and either equation then gives the speed, so a measurement of what comes out of a collision tells you about what you could not see going in.

forms.condition: the second object is initially at rest

concepts.name: Equal masses colliding elastically, $\frac{1}{2}m\kvone^2 = \frac{1}{2}m\kvoneprime^2 + \frac{1}{2}m\kvtwoprime^2 + m\kvoneprime\kvtwoprime\cos(\theta_1 - \theta_2)$
concepts.statement: For two objects of equal mass, conservation of momentum along both axes gives an expression for the initial kinetic energy that carries one extra term beyond the elastic condition. The two statements can both be true only if that extra term is zero, and what follows from that is the whole of what pool players know about angles.

forms.condition: the two objects have equal masses and the second is initially at rest
the two objects have equal masses, the collision is elastic and the second object is initially at rest

concepts.name: Equal masses separate at $\theta_1 - \theta_2 = 90^\circ$
concepts.statement: The extra term can be zero in three ways: the incoming object stops, the incoming object misses, or the angle of separation is ninety degrees. All three are familiar at a pool table, and the third is the one that lets you find the second object’s direction without any further calculation.

forms.condition: the two objects have equal masses, the collision is elastic and both of them move after it

concepts.name: Rocket propulsion
concepts.statement: A rocket, a jet engine, a deflating balloon and a squid all move for the same reason: matter is forcefully ejected from the system, producing an equal and opposite reaction on what remains. The exhaust does not push on the ground, which is why a rocket’s thrust is greater in outer space than on the launch pad.

concepts.name: Thrust, $\kFthrust = \kve\,\Delta m / \kdt$
concepts.statement: The exhaust velocity multiplied by the rate at which mass leaves the rocket is a quantity with the units of newtons, and it is the force the exhaust gases exert on the rocket. The faster the rocket burns its fuel, and the faster the gas leaves, the greater the thrust.

concepts.name: Acceleration of a rocket, $\ka = (\kve / m)(\Delta m / \kdt) - \kg$
concepts.statement: Equating the change in momentum of the whole system over a short time to the impulse of gravity gives a good approximation for the acceleration of what is left of the rocket, $a = (v_{\text{e}}/m)(\Delta m/\Delta t) - g$. It describes a system whose mass changes as it moves.

concepts.name: The three factors in a rocket’s acceleration
concepts.statement: The equation says that a rocket accelerates harder the greater the exhaust velocity, the faster it burns its fuel and the smaller its mass. The last of the three changes as the rocket flies, because most of a rocket is fuel to begin with, so the acceleration increases continuously and reaches a maximum just before the fuel runs out.

concepts.name: Final velocity of a rocket, $\kv = \kve \ln(m_0 / m_{\text{r}})$
concepts.statement: Neglecting air resistance and gravity, the velocity a rocket gains depends only on the exhaust velocity and on the natural logarithm of the ratio of its initial mass to the mass that is left when the fuel is gone. Because the ratio enters through a logarithm, going faster costs a great deal more fuel than you might expect.

forms.condition: air resistance is absent, the gravitational force is neglected and the rocket starts from rest

concepts.name: Why rockets have stages
concepts.statement: Once air resistance and gravity are taken into account, the mass left at burnout can only be about one hundred and eightieth of the initial mass, and it is difficult to build a rocket in which the fuel has a mass 180 times everything else. The answer is to give each stage only part of the final velocity and discard it when its fuel is spent, so that later stages can be smaller.
